text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

Federal Cabinet has approved a major revamp of Australia's environmental law, paving the way to make it simpler for business to secure approval for projects. The proposal, put forward by Environment Minister Robert Hill, removes duplication from federal and state environmental jurisdiction and gives the federal government discretion over all projects of national significance for the environment or for the economy. Page 1.

The Australian Broadcasting Corporation may sell off some of its A$345 million property portfolio to fund a major technology upgrade over the next five years. The proposal, put forward by Russell Balding, acting managing director of the ABC, supports a major upgrade of the national broadcasters' information system to keep it "viable". Page 1.

Australian mining companies have launched an attack on Philippine President Fidel Ramos over access to the Philippine industry. Climax Mining Ltd has urged ministers involved in this week's APEC forum to lobby President Ramos to relax foreign entry rules for international miners wishing to invest in the Asian nation. Page 3.

Federal Industry Minister John Moore, has warned that wages pressure in the construction industry, sparked a pre-Olympics boom, could impact on inflation and interest rates. In an address to the Australian Constructors Association, Moore said the government was relying on executives to keep a lid on wages growth. Page 3.
THE AUSTRALIAN

The summit of 18 Asia Pacific leaders, who account for half the world's output, yesterday vowed to back the push by United States President Bill Clinton for virtually zero tariffs in the information technology area and to open their markets in an effort to "tangibly improve the lives of all our citizens by the turn of the century". Page 1.

Despite A$400 million in federal, state and territory government spending to implement 339 recommendations of the A$30 million Royal Commission into Black deaths in Custody, a report issued by the Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission, released yesterday, shows the rate at which Aborigines are jailed increased 61 percent between 1988 and 1995. The death rate of indigenous inmates also rose sharply. Page 1.

Optus chief executive officer Zigmunt Switkowski, speaking after an Institute of Chartered Accountants lunch in Melbourne, said yesterday that Optus Communications will sue the government if it is required to complete its A$3 billion cable rollout underground, saying it would be too expensive and is not a viable option. Page 3.

Telstra's Big Pond Internet service yesterday announced price cuts to services that will allow home users to enjoy the same high-speed access to the Internet as the business community using an integrated services digital network connection, costing about $130-a-month for 12 hours of access. Page 3.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

In a declaration issued at the end of a one-day summit at the former U.S. naval base at Subic Bay in the Philippines, the 18 Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation forum leaders, including Australia, said the Asia-Pacific regional forum is moving "from vision to action" in its free trade and investment programme. Page 1.

A radical new "once-only" approvals system, to be introduced in New South Wales Parliament early next year in an effort to cut red-tape delays, will see new applicants for all building developments in the state, from the biggest office tower to the smallet suburban home, classified into four simple categories, meaning one-stop approvals. Page 1.

Following the release of the federal government's list of 25 of the top primary schools in New South Wales, which is in direct conflict with the New South Wales Teachers Federation policy, the federation has threatened to ban the basic skills test, taken by more than 120,000 students each year, throwing into doubt the state government's plans for comprehensive reporting on school performance. Page 1.

Following the salmonella food poisoning scare earlier this year, which sparked a national recall of Kraft peanut butter products and created a public relations nightmare for the food giant, Kraft is expected to spend up to A$2 million in the next eight weeks on an advertising campaign designed to ease fears about the safety of the company's peanut butter. Page 3.
THE AGE

Leaders at the Asia-Pacific meeting in the Philippines, have promised to push ahead with cuts to trade barriers as a part of regional trade liberalisation. There is also increasing pressure from some developing countries within APEC for the forum to have an expanded agenda on environmental and social issues. Page A1.

The celebrated Australian movie Shine opened in the U.S. on the weekend to packed cinemas, earning more per screening than any other film in release across theatres. Shine, based on the life of Perth pianist David Helfgott, averaged A$23,429 per screening compared to A$10,829 for Star Trek, A$6,264 for Space Jam and A$4,949 for Ransom with Mel Gibson. Page A1.

Senior Sergeant David Trueman, the head of the Northcote police station and the policeman who publicly promoted the "gay-friendly" image of the Victoria Police, says he has been persecuted by some senior officers for being gay as part of an ongoing campaign in the force against homosexuals. Page A1.

Research conducted by some of Australia's leading economists investigating labour market trends has uncovered evidence revealing the nation's middle-income earners - characterised by two income-earners in a family struggling to pay a mortgage - are increaingly insecure, overworked, plagued by falling incomes and anxiety about job security. Page A1.
